subject: Mixed (Medicine, Surgery, OBG)
paper_title: MedRank Live Test 2 — Medicine / Surgery / OBG

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 70-year-old man presents with sudden right-sided weakness and expressive aphasia, onset exactly 2 hours ago. Non-contrast CT head shows no acute intracranial hemorrhage or early ischemic changes. His blood pressure is 168/94 mmHg, heart rate is 78 bpm, and blood glucose is 142 mg/dL. He has no prior history of stroke, major surgery, or bleeding diathesis. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: IV alteplase (0.9 mg/kg) after confirming no contraindications, followed by stroke unit admission
options.B: Immediate administration of 325 mg oral aspirin and admit to the stroke unit
options.C: Intravenous labetalol to lower systolic blood pressure below 120 mmHg prior to thrombolysis
options.D: Immediate therapeutic anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin drip

questions.explanation: The patient presents with acute ischemic stroke within the standard 0 to 4.5 hour intravenous thrombolysis window (onset 2 hours ago). A non-contrast CT head successfully excludes acute intracranial hemorrhage. His blood pressure is 168/94 mmHg, which is well below the pre-thrombolysis threshold of 185/110 mmHg. Thus, IV alteplase (rtPA) is the standard of care. Aspirin (Option B) should be held for 24 hours post-thrombolysis and is only used acutely if thrombolysis is contraindicated. Lowering BP below 120 mmHg (Option C) compromises cerebral perfusion through the ischemic penumbra; BP lowering is only indicated prior to tPA if BP > 185/110 mmHg. Heparin (Option D) increases hemorrhagic transformation risk without clear clinical benefit in acute ischemic stroke.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 62-year-old male presents with 2 hours of crushing substernal chest pain. ECG demonstrates 2.5 mm ST-segment elevation in leads V1-V4 with ST-segment depression in leads II, III, and aVF. His BP is 82/50 mmHg and HR is 110 bpm. Bedside echocardiogram reveals anterior wall hypokinesis with a normal right ventricle. He is immediately taken for primary PCI, where a total occlusion of the proximal LAD is stented. 4 hours post-procedure, he remains persistently hypotensive (BP 84/52 mmHg) with cold extremities and a cardiac index of 1.7 L/min/m² despite fluid resuscitation of 1.5 L normal saline. Pulmonary artery catheterization shows a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) of 22 mmHg. Which pharmacological agent is most appropriate at this time?

options.A: Invasive fluid bolus with 500 mL 5% Albumin to optimize preload
options.B: High-dose IV Nitroglycerin to reduce elevated left ventricular end-diastolic pressure
options.C: Inotropic support with Dobutamine infusion combined with cautious Vasopressin or Norepinephrine
options.D: Bolus IV Phenylephrine to purely increase systemic vascular resistance

questions.explanation: The patient is experiencing cardiogenic shock complicating an acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Cardiogenic shock is defined hemodynamically by persistent hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg), a cardiac index < 2.2 L/min/m², and elevated filling pressures (PCWP > 15 mmHg). Because his PCWP is already elevated (22 mmHg) and fluid resuscitation has failed to restore blood pressure, additional fluid boluses (Option A) will worsen pulmonary edema. Vasodilators like Nitroglycerin (Option B) will exacerbate profound systemic hypotension. Pure alpha-1 agonists like Phenylephrine (Option D) increase SVR and cardiac afterload, which worsens myocardial wall stress and stroke volume in failing hearts. Dobutamine increases myocardial contractility and cardiac index. When severe hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg) coexists, Norepinephrine is combined with or preferred over Dobutamine to maintain coronary perfusion pressure.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 54-year-old female with long-standing small cell lung carcinoma is admitted with confusion, weakness, and nausea. Laboratory studies show: Serum Sodium 112 mEq/L, Serum Osmolality 238 mOsm/kg, Urine Osmolality 520 mOsm/kg, and Urine Sodium 48 mEq/L. She is lethargic and experiences a generalized tonic-clonic seizure in the emergency room. Which emergency intervention is indicated immediately?

options.A: Fluid restriction to < 500 mL/day and initiation of oral Demeclocycline 300 mg TID
options.B: IV Tolvaptan 15 mg single dose and rapid continuous infusion of 0.9% Normal Saline
options.C: Continuous infusion of 3% Hypertonic Saline targeted to increase serum sodium by 12-16 mEq/L in the first 12 hours
options.D: 3% Hypertonic Saline bolus of 150 mL IV over 20 minutes, repeatable up to 2 times to control seizures

questions.explanation: The patient presents with severe hyponatremia secondary to SIADH associated with small cell lung cancer. The presence of severe neurological symptoms (seizures, altered mental status) makes this a medical emergency requiring rapid, controlled correction of serum sodium to halt cerebral edema. Current consensus guidelines recommend a prompt IV bolus of 150 mL 3% Hypertonic Saline over 20 minutes, which can be repeated once or twice until severe symptoms resolve or serum sodium increases by 4–6 mEq/L. Fluid restriction and Demeclocycline (Option A) are for mild/asymptomatic SIADH. Tolvaptan (Option B) is contraindicated in acute severe symptomatic hyponatremia due to unpredictable correction kinetics. Sodium correction should NOT exceed 8–10 mEq/L in 24 hours (Option C); correcting 12–16 mEq/L in 12 hours carries a high risk of producing irreversible Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome (ODS).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 38-year-old female presents with hyperpigmentation of skin creases, orthostatic hypotension, fatigue, and weight loss over 6 months. Serum Na+ is 128 mEq/L, K+ is 5.8 mEq/L, and morning cortisol at 8 AM is 3.2 mcg/dL (low). ACTH stimulation testing (250 mcg cosyntropin) demonstrates a 30-minute peak cortisol level of 4.1 mcg/dL (normal > 18 mcg/dL). Plasma ACTH is markedly elevated at 450 pg/mL. Thyroid panel reveals TSH 6.8 mIU/L with normal free T4. Anti-21-hydroxylase antibodies are strongly positive. What is the most appropriate management plan regarding corticosteroid and thyroid replacement in this patient?

options.A: Initiate Levothyroxine immediately; hold glucocorticoids until TSH normalizes
options.B: Initiate Hydrocortisone and Fludrocortisone immediately; recheck TSH in 6–8 weeks before deciding on Levothyroxine
options.C: Initiate high-dose Dexamethasone alone; thyroid hormone therapy is strictly contraindicated
options.D: Initiate Levothyroxine and Hydrocortisone simultaneously at full weight-based replacement doses

questions.explanation: This patient has primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease). In Addison's disease, mild elevation of TSH (often 5–10 mIU/L) is very common due to lack of permissive glucocorticoid action on pituitary TSH regulation and co-existing autoimmune thyroiditis. Crucially, giving Levothyroxine before replacing glucocorticoids (Option A or D) can precipitate a life-threatening acute adrenal crisis by increasing hepatic clearance of the minimal remaining endogenous cortisol. Glucocorticoid replacement (Hydrocortisone) along with mineralocorticoid replacement (Fludrocortisone) must be started first. In many patients, replacing glucocorticoids normalizes serum TSH without the need for thyroid hormone replacement.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 65-year-old male presents with a 1-year history of progressive exertional dyspnea and dry cough. Physical exam reveals fine bibasilar velcro crackles and digital clubbing. High-Resolution CT (HRCT) of the chest reveals subpleural, basal-predominant reticular opacities, honeycombing, and traction bronchiectasis without ground-glass opacities. Pulmonary function tests show FVC 58% predicted, FEV1/FVC ratio 0.84, and DLCO 42% predicted. Echocardiogram shows normal LV function and estimated PASP of 32 mmHg. Which treatment regimen is approved to slow the decline of lung function in this patient?

options.A: High-dose Oral Prednisolone combined with Azathioprine and N-acetylcysteine
options.B: Inhaled corticosteroid plus long-acting beta-agonist (ICS/LABA) combined with oral Roflumilast
options.C: Antifibrotic therapy with either Pirfenidone or Nintedanib
options.D: Long-term immunosuppression with Cyclophosphamide and weekly Mycophenolate Mofetil

questions.explanation: The clinical presentation and HRCT pattern establish a definite diagnosis of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF). Antifibrotic agents—Pirfenidone (a TGF-beta and collagen synthesis inhibitor) and Nintedanib (a tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting FGFR, VEGFR, and PDGFR)—are the established targeted therapies shown to slow FVC decline in IPF. Immunosuppressive therapy with Prednisolone, Azathioprine, and N-acetylcysteine (Option A; evaluated in the PANTHER-IPF trial) was shown to increase mortality and hospitalizations in IPF and is strongly contraindicated. ICS/LABA (Option B) is used in obstructive airway diseases (COPD/Asthma). Cyclophosphamide/MMF (Option D) are utilized in connective tissue disease-associated ILD.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 52-year-old male with Child-Pugh Class B alcoholic cirrhosis presents with severe hematemesis. On arrival, BP is 86/52 mmHg, HR is 118 bpm. Two large-bore peripheral IV access lines are secured. Resuscitation with crystalloids and restrictive blood transfusion (target Hb 7–8 g/dL) is initiated. Vasoactive therapy with IV Terlipressin is started. Emergency upper GI endoscopy confirms active bleeding from large esophageal varices, and endoscopic band ligation (EBL) is successfully performed. Prophylactic IV Ceftriaxone is initiated. 48 hours later, he develops new-onset oliguria (urine output 18 mL/hr over 8 hours), serum creatinine rises from baseline 0.9 mg/dL to 2.4 mg/dL. Urine Na+ is < 10 mEq/L, urine osmolality is > 500 mOsm/kg, and renal ultrasound is unremarkable. Fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) is < 0.2%. Dipstick urinalysis shows no protein or red blood cells. Serum creatinine fails to improve after 48 hours of volume expansion with albumin (1 g/kg/day). What is the definitive initial treatment for this patient's renal dysfunction?

options.A: Immediate initiation of continuous venovenous hemodialysis (CVVHD)
options.B: Discontinuation of all vasoactive agents and high-dose IV Furosemide challenge
options.C: Emergency placement of a Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt (TIPS) as first-line medical therapy
options.D: Combination therapy with IV Terlipressin and IV Albumin

questions.explanation: This patient meets criteria for Hepatorenal Syndrome-Acute Kidney Injury (HRS-AKI). Criteria include: Cirrhosis with ascites, AKI according to ICA criteria, no response after at least 48 hours of withdrawal of diuretics and volume expansion with Albumin (1 g/kg/day), absence of shock, no current/recent nephrotoxic drugs, and absence of parenchymal kidney disease. The primary pathophysiological mechanism is severe splanchnic arterial vasodilation leading to compensatory renal vasoconstriction. The first-line medical treatment for HRS-AKI is vasoconstrictor therapy combined with intravenous albumin (Terlipressin + Albumin). Dialysis (Option A) is a bridge to liver transplantation. Loop diuretics (Option B) will worsen renal hypoperfusion. TIPS (Option C) may be considered in refractory cases, but medical therapy with Terlipressin + Albumin is the definitive initial treatment.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 48-year-old male presents with recurrent nasal crusting, purulent epistaxis, chronic sinusitis, a saddle-nose deformity, and non-productive cough with hemoptysis. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates: Serum Creatinine 3.1 mg/dL (up from 0.9 mg/dL 1 month ago), Urinalysis showing dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts. Chest radiography reveals multiple bilateral cavitary nodular infiltrates. Serology demonstrates PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) positivity with high titers. Renal biopsy shows pauci-immune necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis. What is the most effective induction therapy regimen to achieve remission in this patient with organ-threatening disease?

options.A: Glucocorticoids combined with either IV Cyclophosphamide or Rituximab
options.B: High-dose IV Methylprednisolone pulses followed by oral Prednisone alone
options.C: Oral Methotrexate 25 mg weekly combined with Low-dose Prednisone
options.D: Azathioprine combined with Plasmapheresis as sole therapy

questions.explanation: The clinical syndrome combined with c-ANCA/PR3 positivity and pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis confirms Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA). Because this patient has organ-threatening disease (rapidly worsening renal function and pulmonary hemorrhage), induction of remission requires pulse high-dose glucocorticoids combined with EITHER Rituximab OR Cyclophosphamide, as demonstrated in the RAVE and RITUXVAS trials. Steroids alone (Option B) are inadequate for induction. Methotrexate (Option C) is indicated for non-organ-threatening/mild disease with normal renal function (creatinine < 1.5 mg/dL). Azathioprine (Option D) is used for maintenance of remission, not induction.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.question_text: A 42-year-old female presents with a 3-year history of progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids simultaneously, accompanied by nocturnal regurgitation of undigested food and weight loss of 7 kg. High-resolution esophageal manometry (HRM) shows complete absence of peristalsis in the esophageal body and an integrated relaxation pressure (IRP) of 28 mmHg (normal < 15 mmHg) with non-propagated, simultaneous high-amplitude contractions in > 20% of swallows (Type II Achalasia). Barium swallow displays a smooth 'bird's beak' narrowing at the gastroesophageal junction with proximal esophageal dilation. Which treatment provides the most durable long-term symptomatic relief with low complication rates for Type II Achalasia?

options.A: Repeated botulinum toxin injection into the lower esophageal sphincter every 6 months
options.B: Continuous medical therapy with oral isosorbide dinitrate and nifedipine before meals
options.C: Laparoscopic Heller Myotomy with Partial (Dor/Toupet) Fundoplication or Peroral Endoscopic Myotomy (POEM)
options.D: Esophagectomy with gastric pull-up reconstruction

questions.explanation: The findings are definitive for Achalasia cardia (Type II). The definitive treatment options aimed at disrupting the hypertonic lower esophageal sphincter (LES) are Laparoscopic Heller Myotomy (LHM) with a partial antireflux fundoplication (Dor anterior or Toupet posterior) or Peroral Endoscopic Myotomy (POEM). Myotomy provides long-lasting relief (> 85–90% success rate). Botulinum toxin (Option A) is reserved for frail, elderly patients unsuitable for invasive procedures due to high recurrence rates within 6–12 months. Oral nitrates/CCBs (Option B) have poor efficacy and significant side effects. Esophagectomy (Option D) is restricted to end-stage 'sigmoid' esophagus failing multiple prior myotomies.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.question_text: A 58-year-old male undergoes laparoscopic cholecystectomy for acute calculus cholecystitis. On postoperative day 4, he reports progressive right upper quadrant pain, abdominal distension, low-grade fever, and mild jaundice. Vital signs: BP 110/70 mmHg, HR 96 bpm, Temp 38.1°C. Abdominal exam demonstrates localized peritonitis in the right upper quadrant. Ultrasound reveals a 7 cm liquid collection in the gallbladder fossa. Total bilirubin is 3.2 mg/dL, ALP is 340 U/L. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Immediate emergency exploratory laparotomy for abdominal re-exploration and bile duct re-anastomosis
options.B: Percutaneous ultrasound-guided drainage of the fluid collection followed by ERCP with biliary sphincterotomy and stent placement
options.C: Conservative management with IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and observation for 48 hours
options.D: MRCP followed by immediate percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography (PTC) and external biliary drainage

questions.explanation: The patient has a post-cholecystectomy bile leak resulting in a localized intra-abdominal bile collection (biloma). The standard management strategy for a hemodynamically stable patient with a biloma and localized peritonitis involves two main steps: (1) Drainage of the infected biloma via percutaneous ultrasound/CT-guided catheter drainage to control local sepsis, and (2) Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with biliary sphincterotomy +/- plastic stent placement. Immediate exploratory laparotomy (Option A) is overly invasive unless the patient has generalized peritonitis or hemodynamic instability. Conservative observation (Option C) leads to sepsis. PTC (Option D) is reserved for cases where ERCP fails.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old male is diagnosed with adenocarcinoma of the mid-rectum (6 cm from the anal verge). MRI rectum demonstrates a T3 tumor invading through the muscularis propria into the mesorectal fat by 6 mm, with 3 suspicious regional lymph nodes (N1b). The mesorectal fascia (CRM) is clear (> 2 mm margin). Distant metastases are excluded on CT chest/abdomen/pelvis. What is the standard recommended treatment sequence for this patient?

options.A: Upfront total mesorectal excision (TME) followed by adjuvant FOLFOX chemotherapy
options.B: Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) followed by local radical radiation therapy
options.C: Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (or total neoadjuvant therapy) followed by Total Mesorectal Excision (TME) surgery
options.D: Upfront abdominoperineal resection (APR) with permanent colostomy without chemotherapy

questions.explanation: Locally advanced rectal cancer (defined as T3/T4 disease or node-positive N1/N2 disease of the mid-to-low rectum) requires Neoadjuvant Chemoradiotherapy (nCRT) or Total Neoadjuvant Therapy (TNT) prior to definitive surgical resection. Preoperative chemoradiation reduces local recurrence rates significantly compared to postoperative adjuvant therapy. Following nCRT/TNT, Total Mesorectal Excision (TME) is the surgical gold standard. Upfront surgery (Option A) is reserved for early-stage rectal cancer (T1-T2, N0). EMR (Option B) is only suitable for T1 superficial cancers. APR (Option D) is reserved for low rectal cancers invading the anal sphincter complex.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old male is brought to the trauma bay following a high-speed motor vehicle collision. He is pale and confused. Vital signs: BP 76/44 mmHg, HR 135 bpm, RR 26/min. FAST (Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma) scan reveals significant free fluid in the splenorenal recess and rectovesical pouch. Massive transfusion protocol (MTP) is activated. After receiving 2 units of uncrossed O-negative packed red blood cells and 2 units of fresh frozen plasma under pressure, his BP remains 78/46 mmHg. What is the most appropriate immediate surgical procedure?

options.A: Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis to grade solid organ injury
options.B: Diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) to confirm hemoperitoneum red cell count
options.C: Transfer to the angiography suite for pelvic and splenic artery embolization
options.D: Immediate transfer to the operating room for exploratory laparotomy

questions.explanation: According to ATLS guidelines, a trauma patient with blunt abdominal trauma who presents with hemodynamic instability and a positive FAST scan indicating hemoperitoneum that fails to respond to fluid/blood resuscitation (non-responder) requires immediate exploratory laparotomy. Performing a CT scan (Option A) in an unstable patient is dangerous and strictly contraindicated. DPL (Option B) is unnecessary when FAST is already positive. Angiography/Embolization (Option C) is reserved for hemodynamically stable patients with CT-proven vascular extravasation or pelvic fractures.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.question_text: A 68-year-old male smoker with hypertension undergoes routine abdominal ultrasound, which incidentally reveals an infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) measuring 4.2 cm in maximum transverse diameter. He is completely asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.A: Surveillance ultrasound at 6 to 12 month intervals, smoking cessation, and blood pressure control
options.B: Immediate elective Endovascular Aneurysm Repair (EVAR)
options.C: Open surgical repair with a synthetic Dacron graft within 30 days
options.D: Immediate diagnostic catheter angiography to evaluate renal artery involvement

questions.explanation: Elective repair (EVAR or open surgical repair) of an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is indicated when the aneurysm diameter reaches ≥ 5.5 cm in men (or ≥ 5.0 cm in women), or if it expands rapidly (> 1.0 cm/year or > 0.5 cm in 6 months), or becomes symptomatic. For small asymptomatic AAAs measuring 4.0–4.9 cm, randomized controlled trials (UK Small Aneurysm Trial, ADAM trial) have established that surveillance ultrasound every 6–12 months combined with cardiovascular risk reduction (smoking cessation, statin therapy, blood pressure control) is safer than early elective repair. Immediate surgery or EVAR (Options B & C) exposes the patient to unnecessary operative risks. Angiography (Option D) is not a surveillance tool.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.question_text: A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with a painless 2.2 cm solitary hard mass in the upper outer quadrant of her left breast. Core needle biopsy confirms Invasive Ductal Carcinoma, Grade 2. Receptor status: Estrogen Receptor (ER) 90% positive, Progesterone Receptor (PR) 80% positive, HER2/neu negative (IHC 1+). Axillary ultrasound shows normal morphologic lymph nodes with no cortical thickening. Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) performed during breast-conserving surgery (lumpectomy) reveals micrometastasis (0.6 mm) in 1 out of 2 sentinel nodes. What is the most appropriate axillary surgical management?

options.A: Immediate formal Level I and II Axillary Lymph Node Dissection (ALND)
options.B: Completion Level III axillary dissection combined with supraclavicular radiation
options.C: No completion axillary lymph node dissection; proceed to whole-breast irradiation and adjuvant endocrine therapy
options.D: Bilateral sentinel lymph node biopsy to evaluate contralateral risk

questions.explanation: According to the landmark ACOSOG Z0011 trial and IBCSG 23-01 trial, completion Axillary Lymph Node Dissection (ALND) can be safely omitted in patients with T1-T2 invasive breast cancer undergoing breast-conserving surgery with whole-breast radiotherapy who have 1 to 2 sentinel lymph nodes with metastases (including micrometastases ≤ 2 mm), provided there is no clinical or radiologic evidence of bulky nodal disease. Omission of ALND in these patients does not compromise overall survival or disease-free survival, while dramatically reducing the incidence of arm lymphedema and sensory neuropathy. Complete ALND (Options A & B) is unnecessary in this setting.

questions.subject: OBG
questions.question_text: A 32-year-old primigravida at 34 weeks gestation presents with persistent severe frontal headache and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Vital signs: BP 172/114 mmHg (confirmed on two readings 15 minutes apart), HR 88 bpm. Laboratory results: Platelet count 62,000/mcL, AST 210 U/L, ALT 198 U/L, LDH 780 U/L, Total Bilirubin 2.4 mg/dL. Peripheral blood smear demonstrates schistocytes and helmet cells. Serum creatinine is 1.4 mg/dL. Fetal heart tracing reveals a baseline of 140 bpm with moderate variability and late decelerations. What is the immediate, definitive management strategy?

options.A: Administer IV Dexamethasone 12 mg every 12 hours for 48 hours to mature fetal lungs and delay delivery until 37 weeks
options.B: Administer IV Labetalol, initiate IV Magnesium Sulfate prophylaxis, and plan for prompt delivery regardless of gestational age
options.C: Immediate emergency transfusion of 6 units of platelets before any antihypertensive treatment
options.D: Initiate IV Nitroprusside and perform emergency plasmapheresis for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

questions.explanation: This patient meets all criteria for HELLP Syndrome (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets), a severe variant of preeclampsia with severe features. Features include severe hypertension (≥ 160/110 mmHg), neurological symptoms (headache), hepatic distension pain, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, elevated transaminases, and severe thrombocytopenia. HELLP syndrome at or beyond 34 weeks gestation (or at any gestational age with non-reassuring fetal status) is an absolute indication for prompt delivery after maternal stabilization. Immediate management includes: (1) Acute IV antihypertensive therapy, (2) IV Magnesium Sulfate for eclampsia prophylaxis, and (3) prompt delivery (Option B). Delaying delivery for 48 hours for corticosteroids (Option A) is contraindicated in the presence of severe fetal compromise (late decelerations) at 34 weeks. Routine platelet transfusion (Option C) is reserved for platelets < 20,000/mcL or < 50,000/mcL prior to cesarean section.

questions.subject: OBG
questions.question_text: A 29-year-old G3P2 woman at 32 weeks gestation presents with sudden-onset bright red, painless vaginal bleeding. She reports no uterine contractions or trauma. Vital signs: BP 114/72 mmHg, HR 82 bpm. Uterus is soft, non-tender, and relaxed. Fetal heart rate is 145 bpm with reassuring reactive accelerations. What is the most critical initial diagnostic step?

options.A: Immediate digital sterile vaginal examination to evaluate cervical dilation
options.B: Immediate amniotomy to induce labor and tamponade bleeding
options.C: Speculum examination under general anesthesia in the operating room (double setup examination)
options.D: Transabdominal or Transvaginal Ultrasound to locate placental position

questions.explanation: Painless, bright red vaginal bleeding in the third trimester is classic for Placenta Previa until proven otherwise. Performing a digital vaginal examination (Option A) in placenta previa can disrupt placental attachments over the internal os, precipitating catastrophic hemorrhage. Therefore, digital examination is strictly contraindicated prior to ultrasound localization of the placenta. Ultrasound (Option D) is the imaging modality of choice to establish placental position relative to the internal cervical os. Double setup speculum examination (Option C) is obsolete today. Amniotomy (Option B) is contraindicated in placenta previa.

questions.subject: OBG
questions.question_text: A 34-year-old G4P4 gives birth to a 4.3 kg infant following a prolonged labor. 15 minutes after delivery of the intact placenta, profuse vaginal bleeding occurs. Physical examination reveals a soft, boggy uterus palpated 3 cm above the umbilicus. Cumulative blood loss reaches 1,200 mL. Bimanual uterine massage is performed, and IV Oxytocin (40 units in 1 L NS) is infused rapidly along with sublingual Misoprostol 800 mcg. Bleeding continues unabated. Her medical history is significant for severe persistent asthma treated with daily inhaled fluticasone/salmeterol and occasional oral steroid bursts. Vital signs: BP 90/58 mmHg, HR 122 bpm. Which second-line uterotonic agent is strictly contraindicated in this patient?

options.A: Intramuscular Carboprost tromethamine (15-methyl PGF2-alpha)
options.B: Intramuscular Methylergonovine (Methergine)
options.C: Intravenous Tranexamic Acid (TXA)
options.D: Intrauterine Bakri balloon tamponade

questions.explanation: The patient has primary Postpartum Hemorrhage (PPH) secondary to uterine atony. When first-line measures fail, second-line uterotonics are indicated. Carboprost tromethamine (15-methyl PGF2-alpha / Hemabate) causes smooth muscle contraction and potent bronchoconstriction; hence, it is strictly contraindicated in patients with severe asthma. Methylergonovine (Option B) is a vasoconstrictor and is contraindicated in hypertensive disorders, but safe in asthma. Tranexamic Acid (Option C) is an antifibrinolytic recommended within 3 hours of PPH onset in all patients without contraindications. Balloon tamponade (Option D) is a safe non-pharmacological procedural step.

questions.subject: OBG
questions.question_text: A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman (nulliparous, BMI 34 kg/m²) presents with a 2-month history of painless vaginal bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrates an endometrial thickness of 14 mm with a heterogeneous texture. Endometrial biopsy confirms Endometrioid Adenocarcinoma, FIGO Grade 1. Preoperative CT chest/abdomen/pelvis reveals no distant metastases or gross lymphadenopathy. What is the standard surgical staging procedure for this patient?

options.A: Total Abdominal Hysterectomy with Bilateral Salpingo-Oophorectomy (TAH-BSO) alone
options.B: Total Hysterectomy, Bilateral Salpingo-Oophorectomy with Sentinel Lymph Node (SLN) mapping or pelvic/para-aortic lymphadenectomy
options.C: Radical Hysterectomy (Wertheim's procedure) with upper vaginectomy and pelvic lymph node dissection
options.D: High-dose Megestrol acetate hormonal therapy with follow-up biopsy in 6 months

questions.explanation: Endometrial carcinoma is surgically staged according to FIGO guidelines. Standard surgical procedure includes Total Hysterectomy (abdominal, laparoscopic, or robotic) with Bilateral Salpingo-Oophorectomy (TH-BSO) along with retroperitoneal lymph node evaluation—either via Sentinel Lymph Node (SLN) mapping or systematic pelvic and para-aortic lymphadenectomy. Omission of lymph node assessment (Option A) leads to understaging. Radical hysterectomy (Option C) is reserved for cervical cancer or endometrial cancer with explicit stromal invasion of the cervix (Stage II). Hormonal therapy (Option D) is reserved for young women desiring fertility preservation.

questions.subject: OBG
questions.question_text: A 31-year-old nulligravid female presents with severe dysmenorrhea, deep dyspareunia, and cyclic dyschezia (painful defecation during menses) for 2 years. Bimanual pelvic examination reveals fixed retroverted uterus with tender nodularity along the uterosacral ligaments and left adnexal fullness. Transvaginal pelvic ultrasound reveals a 5 cm ground-glass homogenous hypoechoic cyst in the left ovary with low-level internal echoes and no solid internal vascular components. CA-125 is 58 U/mL (mildly elevated). She desires future fertility. What is the gold standard diagnostic and therapeutic intervention for this patient?

options.A: Diagnostic laparoscopy alone followed by 6 months of Leuprolide acetate without surgery
options.B: Left unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy to completely eradicate the affected tissue
options.C: Laparoscopic surgical excision (cystectomy) of the endometrioma and ablation/excision of deep infiltrating endometriotic implants
options.D: Transvaginal ultrasound-guided aspiration of the ovarian cyst contents followed by sclerotherapy

questions.explanation: The clinical presentation and TVUS findings ('ground-glass' appearance characteristic of an endometrioma) confirm Endometriosis with Deep Infiltrating Endometriosis (DIE). Diagnostic laparoscopy with histopathological evaluation remains the gold standard for diagnosis. In patients desiring fertility preservation, laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy (surgical excision of the endometrioma wall) is superior to simple fenestration/drainage or ablation because excision yields lower recurrence rates and higher spontaneous pregnancy rates. Oophorectomy (Option B) is unnecessarily aggressive for a 31-year-old wanting fertility. Simple aspiration (Option D) carries a nearly 100% recurrence rate. Medical therapy alone (Option A) does not eliminate endometriomas > 3 cm or deep retrovaginal implants.

questions.subject: OBG
questions.question_text: A 26-year-old female presents with oligomenorrhea (3–4 menses per year), facial hirsutism (Ferriman-Gallwey score 12), and difficulty conceiving for 18 months. BMI is 31 kg/m². Pelvic ultrasound demonstrates expanded ovaries bilaterally with > 20 peripheral follicles measuring 2–9 mm arranged in a 'string-of-pearls' pattern and an increased stromal volume. Serum Fasting Glucose is 108 mg/dL, and 2-hour OGTT is 158 mg/dL (impaired glucose tolerance). Serum prolactin, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, and TSH are normal. What is the first-line ovulation induction agent for fertility in this patient?

options.A: Letrozole 2.5 mg daily for 5 days starting on cycle days 3 to 5
options.B: Clomiphene Citrate 50 mg daily for 5 days
options.C: Metformin 850 mg BID monotherapy without ovulation inductors
options.D: Exogenous Human Menopausal Gonadotropin (hMG) injections

questions.explanation: The patient meets all 3 Rotterdam criteria for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS). Based on current international evidence-based guidelines, Letrozole (an aromatase inhibitor) is the FIRST-LINE agent for ovulation induction in women with PCOS, offering significantly higher live-birth rates and cumulative ovulation rates compared to Clomiphene Citrate (Option B), particularly in obese women (BMI > 30 kg/m²). Metformin monotherapy (Option C) improves metabolic profile but is inferior for ovulation induction. Gonadotropins (Option D) are second-line options when oral ovulation inductors fail due to high risks of OHSS and multiple gestations.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 58-year-old male renal transplant recipient on Tacrolimus and Mycophenolate Mofetil presents with a 3-day history of low-grade fever, severe headache, confusion, and ataxia. On physical exam: Temp 38.4°C, Kernig sign is positive. CT head shows no mass lesion or midline shift. Lumbar puncture is performed. CSF analysis reveals: Opening pressure 240 mmH2O, WBC count 480 cells/mcL with 82% lymphocytes, Protein 185 mg/dL, Glucose 32 mg/dL (serum glucose 105 mg/dL). CSF Gram stain shows intracellular and extracellular short, Gram-positive rods with tumbling motility at room temperature. What empirical intravenous antibiotic regimen must be initiated immediately?

options.A: Ceftriaxone 2g IV q12h + Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h
options.B: Acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV q8h + High-dose Fluconazole 800 mg IV daily
options.C: Ampicillin 2g IV q4h + Ceftriaxone 2g IV q12h + Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h
options.D: Meropenem 2g IV q8h alone as monotherapy

questions.explanation: The CSF analysis along with Gram stain showing short Gram-positive rods displaying tumbling motility at room temperature identifies *Listeria monocytogenes* meningitis. *Listeria* selectively infects immunocompromised individuals (e.g., renal transplant patients). Third-generation cephalosporins (Ceftriaxone / Cefotaxime) have NO activity against *Listeria monocytogenes*. Therefore, empirical coverage for community-acquired bacterial meningitis in immunocompromised patients or adults > 50 years MUST include high-dose IV Ampicillin (2g q4h) specifically added to standard empiric therapy (Ceftriaxone + Vancomycin). Acyclovir/Fluconazole (Option B) does not treat *Listeria*.
